items.title: Sublime Seixas Becomes Youngest-Ever Winner of IL Lombardia with Huge Solo Move
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Paul Seixas reaffirms huge potential with stomping solo victory, capturing the first Monument success of his career.
items.lbText:
Paul Seixas wins Il Lombardia (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Paul Seixas further underlined his staggering talent with an assured win at Il Lombardia , taking the first Monument win of his career and becoming the youngest-ever winner.

The 20 year old drove forward with 19.2km to go to drop most of the other big contenders on the Civiglio, the penultimate climb of the day. He went over the top well clear of European championships runner-up Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), with the latter being replaced by Vuelta winner Enric Mas (Movistar)

Seixas powered up the second and final ascent of the San Fermo Della Battaglia, with Mas dropping Ciccone in a bid to close up to him.

However he was far too strong, racing in well clear and savoring the biggest win of his career.

Mas raced in for second place, 48 seconds back, with Ciccone taking third in his final race for his team.

Seixas looked stunned by what he had done, and said that things hadn’t really sunk in by the time he did the post-race interview.

“It is crazy. I think I don’t realize [it] for now,” he said. “Everything went perfect, the team did a great, awesome job. Everyone pushed more than what they had to do.”

His Decathlon CMA CGM team did indeed dedicate themselves to him, helping him to save energy until it most counted.

“I had amazing legs. I had the feeling that today was a great day,” he continued. “I managed to make the difference at the moment I choose. Maybe a bit earlier because I felt like the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb, for me at least, to make the difference.

“So I had to accelerate early, maybe a bit too early. There were some not really steep parts, so I had to manage really well my effort and accelerate in the hard parts. I did the best TT I could, me against myself. It was crazy.”

New European champion Remco Evenepoel had to be satisfied with fourth place, something well below his pre-race ambitions. He crashed in Il Lombardia in his 2020 debut, going over the side of a bridge and falling several meters to the ground.

He fractured his pelvis and has tried to win the race several time since. He was second to Tadej Pogačar in 2024 and 2025 and with Pogačar absent due to injury, he felt he might have his big victory this time around.

That optimism was furthered by his victory in the Euros last weekend but, once the pressure was applied, he found himself slipping backwards and losing contact with the other big challengers.

Just as was the case at the worlds, he dangled off the back of the groups his rival were in, but eventually fought his way forward again towards the end. He led the sprint in for fourth place, 1:20 back, with new world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG) continuing his stomping end of season with fifth place.

“I think I had bad position going into the penultimate climb,” he said. “I made a bit of an effort to come to the front and went a little deep on the wheel of Paul and paid for it.

“I felt really good today. But then that climb, I went into the red. That was it.”

The final Monument of the season was, as ever, a very tough one. It packed in 4662 vertical meters over 239km, and was enlivened by a big breakaway sparked off 211 kilometers out by Uno-X Mobility rider Johannes Kulse.

Andrea Mifsud (Team Polti VisitMalta), Micahel Leonard, Ben O’Connor (Jayco-AlUla) and Maxime Decomble (Groupama-FDJ United) got across, while Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain Victorious), Sylvain Moniquet (Cofidis), Fausto Masnada (MBH Bank Csb Telecom Fort), George Bennett, Pau Martí (NSN), Gijs Leemreize (Picnic PostNL) and Louis Vervaeke (Soudal Quick-Step) did likewise soon afterwards.

Julien Bernard (Lidl-Trek) and Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) made it 14 and together they build a lead of almost three minutes.

O’Connor hacked down the break’s size when he set a furious pace on the Ghisallo. Their lead was 1:29 with 61.5km remaining, with the pace heating up behind when Louis Barre (Visma-Lease a Bike) went all out to platform a huge move by Matteo Jorgenson.

The American was joined by compatriots Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) and Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG), as well as the Italian Christian Scaroni (XDS Astana).

However Giulio Pellizzari put in a huge effort and brought them back several kilometers later, then continued to plough along at the front for Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe. Simmons had been the fastest up the Ghisallo but had the misfortune to experience a mechanical, ruining his chances.

Pellizzari continued to set a determined pace on the climb of San Fermo Della Battaglia and put Jorgenson, Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Juan Ayuso (Lidl-Trek) and Lenny Martinez (Bahrain-Victorious) out the back. His efforts ensured the break had just 44 seconds crossing the finish line with 21.8km to go, and while Leonard pushed clear alone soon afterwards on the climb of Civiglio, he was reeled in soon afterwards.

Isaac Del Toro was the big hope for UAE and Adam Yates did most of the work on that climb. However it was Seixas who was strongest. He stomped away with 19.2km remaining, Pidcock and Ciccone clinging on briefly before being forced to slow.

Pidcock’s place in the chase was taken by soon afterwards by Mas, with the Vuelta winner dropping Ciccone on the San Fermo Della Battaglia but having zero success in trying to get back up to Seixas.

The Frenchman was absolutely flying. He may have been the youngest rider in the whole race but he was far above the level of the rest.

“It is a dream. Today my legs made me dream today and then I had an opportunity,” he smiled.

“I really trained hard for this. It is incredible.”

It is, and it set things up for some fascinating clashes with Pogačar next season.

Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Procycling) was sixth, with nine riders in total in this group.

items.title: Il Lombardia: Paul Seixas puts in stunning solo ride to claim first Monument
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
French prodigy Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) became the youngest winner in Il Lombardia history on Sunday, going solo 18km from the line to take a stunning win and cap an outstanding season.

The 20-year-old had his team working on the front all day, but Seixas himself stayed patient until the crucial moment, putting in one big acceleration on the Civiglio climb that no one could follow for more than a minute or two. From there, despite being chased by some of the strongest riders in the world, the Frenchman could not be reeled back in.

Vuelta a España winner Enric Mas (Movistar) ditched the uncooperative Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) in the finale to try and chase down Seixas solo, but his efforts were futile as the Frenchman soloed to victory by 49 seconds.

Mas settled for second, as Ciccone rolled in a few seconds behind him to cap off his career with Lidl-Trek with a third place.

Pre-race favourite Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) sprinted to fourth from the chase group as an unsatisfactory consolation prize, after being visible and active all day but ultimately not being able to react to the crucial move.

Earlier in the day, a 14-man breakaway was up the road for most of the day, with seven riders surviving into the final 20km, but Seixas' move spelled the end of their day, with Michael Leonard (EF Education-EasyPost) the final rider to be caught.

With his win just two weeks after his 20th birthday, Seixas becomes the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia, and the fourth youngest men's Monument victor in history.

"It's crazy. I think I don't realise for now," he said at the finish. "Everything went perfect. The teammates [did a] great, awesome job. Everyone pushed more than what they had to do, and yeah, I had amazing legs.

"I had the feeling that today was a great day, and I managed to make the difference at the moment I chose, maybe a bit earlier, because I felt like the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb – for me at least – to make the difference, so I had to accelerate early, maybe a bit too early. There was some not really steep parts, so I had to manage really efforts and accelerate in the hard parts.

"Then I did the best I could, a TT, me against myself and yeah, it was crazy."

He knew he had a decent gap, but said it was "not enough to think about the win before the end of the last climb".

"Then at the end of the last climb I started believing and I just had to not make mistakes on the downhill, so I was careful. I don't realise [what I've done], I think."

After the 239km race eventually got underway after the peloton staged a protest about safety by delaying the start, business as usual resumed with the attacks starting straight out of the neutral zone. Martin Marcellusi (Bardiani CSF 7 Saber) was the very first rider to attack, but the day's break wasn't going to get away that easily, and the battle continued all the way up the opening climbs.

An initial group of five got away midway up the Selvino climb, but the fight was continuing behind them with multiple counter-attacks, and the leaders were joined over the top of the ascent to make it a 14-rider break.

The riders were: Ben O'Connor (Jayco AlUla), Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain-Victorious), Michael Leonard (EF Education-EasyPost), Maxime Decomble (Groupama-FDJ United), Johannes Kulset (Uno-X Mobility), Andrea Mifsud (Polti VisitMalta), George Bennett, Pau Marti (NSN), Fausto Masnada (MBH Bank CSB Telecom Fort), Gijs Leemreize (Picnic PostNL), Sylvain Moniquet (Cofidis), Louis Vervaeke (Soudal-QuickStep), Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Julien Bernard (Lidl-Trek).

With most big teams represented, the peloton seemed relatively happy to let this break go, and they soon built a gap of two minutes – though they weren't given much more than that as UAE, Red Bull and Decathlon controlled the gap.

Back in the peloton, a mechanical and bike change for world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) saw him dropped from the peloton and facing a substantial chase back on, but he made it back to the bunch and his teammates without too much trouble.

The longest climb of the day, the Valpiana, passed without much action, with the breakaway riders managing their efforts and keeping the gap stable towards the 150km to go mark. On the long descent, however, the breakaway actually managed to grow their advantage over the peloton, stretching the gap out to three minutes for the first time all day as the still 14-strong group took on the long flat before the next climb.

Things were certainly not slow in the peloton heading into the final 120km, but teams and riders seemed to be just making sure they didn't do too much, too soon with the decisive climbs all still to come.

It did not take too long for the pace to kick back up in the bunch, though, and the gap started slowly falling again on the Giovenzana climb as UAE lined up at the front of the peloton and started burning through riders.

With 90km to go, the break briefly split apart, and whilst they reunited relatively quickly, it was the first sign of the leaders perhaps getting ready to attack and take opportunities. The long, flat, lake-side stretch before the Madonna del Ghisallo gave the break a chance to reset and regroup, though the peloton were winding up towards full pace in their pursuit.

The break hit the Madonna del Ghisallo 2:30 ahead of the peloton, with the stronger climbers quickly coming to the fore and O'Connor settling the early pace. His efforts saw Tiberi among the first riders to be dropped, and soon hardly anyone could hold onto the Australian's wheel, with him and Leemreize pulling out a gap on the early slopes. Leonard was able to pace back up to them, making it three in the lead, but Leemreize soon dropped back as the leaders' gap fell back below two minutes.

That shrinking of the gap was because, just as had happened in the break, the bunch hitting the climb signalled the arrival of the favourites and climbers at the front of the peloton; no one was quite attacking, but Red Bull and UAE were both battling for supremacy on the front of the group.

O'Connor and Leonard were rejoined by five riders from the break halfway up the climb, but the seven leaders were now less than a minute and a half ahead of the bunch, led by Red Bull's Giulio Pellizzari.

The attacks began near the top when Louis Barre (Visma-Lease a Bike) led out a big move from Matteo Jorgenson, with his compatriots Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) and McNulty on his wheel, plus XDS Astana's Christian Scaroni. The quartet went clear over the top of the climb, and though they didn't have a huge gap on the peloton, it left Evenepoel, Red Bull and Decathlon with work to do on the descent.

Red Bull enlisted Primož Roglič to help in the chase, and with 50km to go, the attackers – with Masnada from the break now tagging along too – were 13 seconds ahead of the main group, with the leaders another 50 seconds up the road. The attackers were caught only a few kilometres later, though, and there was a brief rest as the favourites weighed up their next moves.

This slight lull saw the leaders' gap go back out, and they still had 1:20 with 35km to go as the race entered the finishing circuit and the final three climbs. After looking strong, Simmons had a poorly timed mechanical at the start of the circuit and dropped out of the reduced bunch and faced a tough chase back on.

All the favourite teams were amassed at the front of the peloton, but there was still a lot of work to be done to actually bring the leaders back if the big names were to contest the finish. On the first time up the San Fermo della Battaglia climb, Pellizzari hit the front once again to wind things up for Evenepoel, with McNulty, Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5), Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and Seixas behind them.

Pellizzari paced to the top of the climb, and his efforts took a big chunk out of the leaders' advantage, though they were still working hard up front to try and give themselves as big a chance as possible of holding on. The gap sat at 40 seconds with 20km remaining.

On the Civiglio climb, Leonard pushed on up ahead to be the final survivor of the break, but the favourites were hot on his heels as Paul Seixas made his first serious move towards the top, which reeled Leonard back in but – more crucially – saw Evenepoel struggling to hold on at the back of the group.

Seixas' move was not explosive, but a steady winding up of his speed was an effort that only Pidcock and Ciccone could follow, with Evenepoel and Del Toro noticeably off the pace. It didn't take long for Seixas to drop his companions, too, and the young Frenchman went solo with 18km remaining. He went over the top of the climb with a gap of 25 seconds on Ciccone and Mas, which was not insurmountable, but Seixas looked much stronger than the riders trying to chase him down, and his gap only grew as he settled into his rhythm.

Ciccone and Mas weren't working well together behind, so Mas pushed on solo without the Italian, but even that was fairly futile as he was still nearly a minute down on Seixas with 5km to go. That gap meant the Frenchman was able to savour his victory as he soloed to the line, capping a phenomenal season with an historic first Monument victory.

Mas rolled in for second just ahead of Ciccone, whilst Evenepoel sprinted it out for fourth from the large chasing group, but ultimately could not live up to his favourite status.

items.title: BTCC Brands Hatch GP: Moffat leads throughout to beat Ingram in qualifying race
Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore GP pole
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Max Verstappen’s perfect Singapore weekend continued as he claimed pole position for the grand prix, beating the Ferraris in Formula 1 qualifying.

Verstappen’s first Q3 flying lap - a 1m31.373s - ended up being good enough to top qualifying, following on from his sprint race pole and victory.

Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari was his closest challenger, setting a lap 0.054s slower than Verstappen’s. Lewis Hamilton made it two Ferraris in the top three, just 0.069s adrift of Leclerc.

Kimi Antonelli will line up on the second row alongside Hamilton, having been fourth-quickest in the upgraded Mercedes.

The McLaren drivers, who collided in the sprint race, will share the third row.

Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were fifth and seventh in qualifying with George Russell between them in the older-spec Mercedes, but Russell will move to the back of the grid with an engine penalty.

Pierre Gasly won F1’s midfield fight in qualifying, qualifying eighth (which is set to become seventh on the grid) and beating the Racing Bulls duo of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad.

Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg was the quickest driver knocked out in Q2, 0.182s away from a place in Q3.

Haas drivers Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon were 12th and 13th ahead of Carlos Sainz’s Williams, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto and Alpine’s Franco Colapinto, over a second slower than team-mate Gasly.

Both Aston Martins fell in the first stage of qualifying after Fernando Alonso reported a turbo issue, which he thinks means his team should change his power unit for the race.

He qualified 17th, just ahead of Alex Albon’s Williams and still seven tenths clear of team-mate Lance Stroll, just as he was in sprint qualifying.

Sergio Perez led Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas, the pair the two slowest drivers to set a lap in qualifying.

Isack Hadjar’s nightmare Saturday in Singapore continued as he ground to a halt before he could even set a timed lap in Q1.

Hadjar managed to return his Red Bull to the garage, then came out again and encountered an issue again. He will start among the penalised drivers at the back of the field on Sunday.

items.title: Stewards rule Piastri shares blame for Norris clash
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Formula 1’s Singapore Grand Prix stewards determined that both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri contributed to their last-lap sprint race collision, so ruled that no further action was necessary.

The stewards said Piastri hadn’t expected Norris to overtake him, but he "noticed [Norris] on the inside and attempted to leave space".

"[Norris] said that he saw an opportunity to overtake and said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of [Piastri] prior to the apex, and therefore expected to be left space.

"As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated, so he had to use the inside kerb and braked, and a collision occurred.

"The stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision.

"Therefore, the stewards determined to take no further action."

Norris is right that he had his front axle ahead of the mirror of Piastri’s sister car at the apex of Turn 5, so he satisfies that aspect of F1’s racing rules.

But it does not appear Piastri - who was caught unawares by the divebomb - had means of leaving more space at that corner; so once he turned in, a collision became inevitable.

Given the stewards stated "both drivers had contributed to the incident", we can infer that Piastri’s not anticipating the overtake and leaving enough space is what he did wrong - whereas Norris was ambitious with his move and had to climb onto the inside kerb to try to complete it.

The start of Norris’s interview with F1 broadcaster Viaplay after the sprint race made his feelings clear.

Norris was asked: "You'll surely always want to finish as high as possible, but it’s also a sprint, P4 and P5 and it was your team-mate in front of you... Wasn’t it too unnecessary, that move?"

He replied: "What, to go for a big gap? To overtake?". He followed up: "What's the title name of the race?"

The interviewer replied, "sprint", to which Norris said: "Sprint. What’s [the word] after sprint?" - "race" came the reply.

Norris smiled: "Wow! Good job. It’s a race".

"We were just stuck the whole race and the last lap there was a big opportunity into [Turn] 5 so I went for it," Norris said in the media pen.

"The gap closed a bit more than I would have liked and obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing - so I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one. But it was a big gap so I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team."

Piastri said "it’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, not that bothered either way, just a lot of work for the team to get both cars fixed, just a shame for the team".

Meanwhile, Liam Lawson, having been shown a replay of the incident by Sky Sports F1’s Karun Chandhok, mused: "On the last lap, it’s not for many points; I don't think it's worth it".

Perez dodges serving penalty for Stroll clash

There was a slightly unusual decision made in the assessment of another of the sprint’s incidents.

Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll collided on the opening lap of the race when Perez tried to pass on the inside of the Turn 16 right-hander.

The stewards felt Stroll had turned in reasonably for the corner and Perez was predominantly to blame after having a lock-up.

They considered the tricky conditions reasonable mitigation and wanted to issue Perez with a five-second penalty instead of the usual 10.

But Perez retired from the race - and according to the stewards a five-second penalty does not typically convert to a grid drop.

Had it been a 10-second penalty, this would be different. So Perez escapes sanction for the clash.

items.title: Things from the Aaron Boone era that I’m sick of watching
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
This year’s ALDS sweep at the hands of the Rays felt like a culmination for the Aaron Boone era Yankees. I’m not sure it will be a culmination of his managerial tenure as I could definitely see the team keeping him, but those three games felt like everything that has gone wrong in a Yankees’ playoff exit from 2018 to now all rolled into one. There were mental mistakes, sloppy play, and bats going cold all at once.

I think it would be unfair to say that Boone hasn’t grown at all since taking the job. Early in his tenure, I used to get frustrated by him sticking with a pitcher too long trying to steal an extra out or two. These days, it seems pretty rare that those instances happen. However, any growth from him is overshadowed by the frustration that I share with many other Yankee fans.

In watching this year’s playoff defeat, my mind couldn’t help but keep going over the things that went wrong that I could see coming, because all of Boone’s teams seem to suffer in these ways. Whether or not the Yankees do bring Aaron Boone back, I personally am out, and it would take a massive change of fortune to change that. Here are the reasons why.

For one, his teams seem to play with just no sense of fundamentals. I am an analytically-inclined fan, so when I say this, I don’t meant that they don’t bunt enough or that they need to learn to go the other way and hit singles, because I think there are logical reasons that make it easier said than done against the pitchers of today. However, there are some baseball things that happen in the heat of the moment of a game that don’t make sense no matter your way of thinking.

Austin Wells getting thrown out try to stretch a double into a triple in Game 1 of the ALDS is the perfect example. “Don’t make the last out of the inning at third base” is a longtime baseball axiom that makes perfect sense. With two outs, you can’t score on a sacrifice fly or any other kind of productive out, so those 90 feet matter way less than just having a chance with a runner in scoring position. Yet in the heat of the game, Wells seemingly wasn’t even thinking about that, never mind the fact that he ran through Luis Rojas’ stop sign too.

I feel like I regularly watch the Yankees allow opposing runners to take extra bases because a fielder tries for an out at home that has like a five percent chance at happening rather than throwing ahead of the runner, holding them, and living to fight for another day. Or, an infielder will try and make a rushed and/or spectacular throw to try and complete a double play leading to an error, and a runner getting an extra base (à la Jazz Chisholm Jr. in Game 2). I know it’s probably hard to think about these things in the moment and your instincts will kick in to some degree, but it feels like the Yankees regularly disadvantage themselves by going to the spectacular instead of sticking to basics.

Relatededly, I have another issue with the defense in general. Anthony Volpe went from winning a Gold Glove as a rookie to looking like a shortstop novice in just two seasons. It’s cost the Yankees some playoff games, including the infamous 2024 World Series Game 5 meltdown. Again, errors are something that are going to occur no matter what, but the Boone Yankees have been so sloppy so often.

That sloppiness also almost always comes to a head during an almost annual mid-season — usually around June or July — swoon.

Another baseball saying is that every team wins 50 and loses 50, and your season is decided by what you do in the rest of the games. For the most part, that holds true and I don’t think there’s any manager who could’ve snapped their fingers and won 110 games with any of Boone’s Yankees teams. Every team is going to slump. However, why is it that every Boone team will start off hot and then go through about a month where they appear to forget how to play baseball?

This year, they went 12-14 in June. If you expand that out to a couple days either side of the month, they had a 15-20 stretch. In 2025, they were under .500 in all of June and July. They were under .500 in July 2024, and that includes a five-game winning streak at the end of the month. They were on pace for 122 wins in mid-June 2022 and ended up winning under 100.

Again, I recognize that every team is going to have some slumps. The MLB-best Brewers were just barely over .500 after April and ended up with 103 wins. No team is going to put up exactly even .600 winning percentages every month — even the 1998 Yankees played a few ticks below that pace in September. However, I would appreciate if the Yankees stop having a stretch that obviously foreshadows what is going to happen that October.

Another issue that has played out in the postseason, but sometimes appears in the regular season as well is that the Boone Yankees’ teams never get the last laugh. I don’t mean this just in a “they haven’t won the World Series” sense, but they always seem to be the team that ends with with egg on their face.

In 2020, they got into it with the Rays after Aroldis Chapman airmailed a pitch over Mike Brosseau’s head, leading to a verbal back and forth between the two teams, on the field and in the media. What happens that October? The Yankees lose to the Rays after … Mike Brosseau homers off Aroldis Chapman.

In a 2021 Subway Series game, Francisco Lindor made allusions to what he perceived as the Yankees’ stealing signs. Giancarlo Stanton chirped him back after he hit a home run, leading to the benches clearing. However, what ended up deciding the game? Lindor’s third homer of the game.

Beyond just losing every postseason under Boone, the Yankees constantly end up the butt of jokes, and frankly I’m done with it.

items.title: Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out
items.content: <article>Red Bull's Max Verstappen wins an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after George Russell crashes out of the lead.</article>
items.lbText:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after Mercedes driver George Russell crashed out of the lead.

Russell was leading in tricky conditions, with half the track dry and half wet, when he got a little too wide at the final corner at the end of the first lap.

He lost control of his Mercedes, which spun across the track into the inside wall, before bouncing back again to the outside, the rest of the field somehow avoiding him.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second having made a superb start from sixth on the grid with team-mate Charles Leclerc third.

A final-lap collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri at Turn Five promoted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli to fourth place.

In combination with Russell's retirement, that extends the Italian's championship lead to 89 points.

A chaotic race saw the start delayed by 30 minutes by a tropical downpour, and then Verstappen navigating a safety car period following Russell's accident, a restart, and initial pressure from Hamilton to eventually ease away into a comfortable lead.

It was the Dutchman's second Formula 1 win in seven days, after his maiden victory this season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the first time he has won in Singapore.

The rain before the start hit only parts of the track. The second sector stayed dry while the first sector, particularly Turns Two and Three, were soaking wet with standing water.

Once the rain abated, the field did two laps behind a safety car to check conditions before racing began with a standing start.

Russell gave himself a golden opportunity to breathe some life into his almost-extinguished title hopes when he beat Verstappen off the line and took the lead into the first corner.

But after leading the first lap, he made a mistake at the final corner.

Russell said: "I just misjudged it, got more power than I was expecting from the battery, got a little wider than I expected and touched the white line. Rule number one in the wet is don't touch the white line. Very silly mistake."

That left Verstappen in front, with Hamilton behind. But after the seven-time champion pursued his erstwhile 2021 title rival for a few laps, the Red Bull began to ease away and was clearly in control, leading Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli.

With overtaking difficult around Marina Bay, the field was static until the closing stages.

Leclerc was struggling, and he began to be caught by the McLarens and Antonelli.

Norris had been pressuring Piastri for some laps before the Australian also began to close in on Leclerc, and Antonelli, struggling with oversteer in the early laps, picked up the pace.

On the final lap, Norris made a better exit out of Turn Three and saw an opportunity to try to pass Piastri at Turn Five, but Piastri defended his position robustly, the cars touched, and spun in unison.

Norris was initially far enough alongside to make a legitimate passing attempt, but having apparently tried to back out of the move, not so at the apex to satisfy the driving standards rules.

But the criticism of Norris will be that he miscalculated the risk-reward, that it was an ill-advised, marginal move against his team-mate for little gain - a point was at stake - and none for the team, as it would have not changed their collective points total.

The stewards investigated the incident but took no action on the basis that both drivers had contributed to the incident.

Piastri, who hit the barriers, was out on the spot, but Norris was able to keep going, although he fell down to eighth, behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.

items.title: On the Yankees’ playoff failures and the agony of apathy
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
I try very hard to fight back against apathy. In politics, the economy, media, the world begs for your apathy. Don’t make a fuss, let it all just happen. It’s all going According to Plan. The state apparatus depends on your apathy. Do not give them that gift.

And yet, not quite 48 hours after the Yankees once again lost in the ALDS, lost to a team seeded higher than them, lost to a team that is just so fundamentally annoying that thinking about them raises my blood pressure a point or two…I don’t feel much at all.

I’ve always tried to hedge my reactions to bad sports news. The Don LeGreca-style rants make for good radio and some of the longer, more unhinged comments we get here are fun to scroll past, but at the end of the day I consume baseball for my own entertainment. Letting yourself get mad over something you say you enjoy while having 0 control over it hasn’t made a whole lot of sense to me. Let sports lift you up, not press you down.

And true to form, I’m not mad about the 2026 Yankees. I’m beige. The Yankees dogwalked the Red Sox last week only to find themselves canine-ized by the Rays, swept out of the ALDS in what’s actually a worse result than last year. (They lasted a whole four games against the Blue Jays!) Aaron Boone put the worst leadoff hitter in baseball atop the lineup, telling us that he liked the potential for action on the basepaths ahead of the only batter who showed up in the series, and that leadoff hitter went 0-for-5 as the team died—with him as the final out—because of course he did.

I don’t quite know why I’m so numb to all of this. The Yankees won 93 games, the second-best record in the AL, without the game’s best player, while actively rehabbing three pitchers in their starting rotation, while Austin Wells was locked in the trunk of a car for four months, while shortstop was an open question until the season’s final few weeks. It should be kind of remarkable that they were even in the dance in the first place?

But the AL was so bad, the table so uncompetitive, that the Yankees didn’t really outrun the other guy being chased by the bear. There was no bear at all. The team wasn’t good enough to chase down the Rays, dooming themselves to an additional two playoff games while the Rays got to rest, prepare, and welcome the Yankees to the Trop for the start of the series. The same offense we’d seen sleepwalk through the year for weeks at a time showed themselves, they lost, and I don’t really care.

Supposedly at the staff level the organization is starting to pick at itself like an under-stimulated pet bird. This annual tradition of “just be good enough to make it before 26 people who should be among the best in the world at what they do collectively forget what their jobs are” might finally be sinking in. At the top level though we’ll be told not to worry, There is A Plan, these guys are having good at bats actually, it’s right in front of us.

Congratulations to the New York Yankees. You’ve managed to accomplish something my government and AI companies haven’t. Sure, man, whatever you say, I shrug my shoulders and I walk down the street.

items.title: Winners and losers from F1's wet Singapore GP sprint race
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
But that still demanded cool heads of the 22 drivers - some of whom were more successful at keeping cool than others.

Here's our pick of winners and losers from the sixth and final sprint race of the 2026 Formula 1 season.

“I just misjudged it,” George Russell said of his early race-ending Singapore crash.

Even if this is likely to make no difference to his ever-dwindling title hopes, Russell is in a position where, for his own sake, he needs to end the year on a high.

Grabbing the lead from Verstappen at the start in the sprint looked like the perfect way to do that before a grid penalty hobbles the rest of his weekend.

But the heavy crash - which he put down to having more power than expected from the battery exiting the final corner and then touching the white line as he ran a little wide - put paid to that in a very painful way.

“It's a very, very silly mistake,” he said. “Overly confident. Think it's my first crash of the year. It's annoying to happen from that position.”

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (4th)

This was a quintessential ‘when it’s your year, it’s your year’ kind of day for Kimi Antonelli.

He did nothing remarkable - which in itself is good because evidently these were conditions it was easy to trip up in - and yet took another little step towards his world championship.

His chief title ‘rival’ Russell crashed out of a winning position on the first lap. Then, at the very end, two cars ahead of him were removed by a needless collision.

Apart from keeping the car on the road this is the easiest progress Antonelli will make all season - and it almost ended in an unlikely sprint podium, such was Leclerc’s trouble by the end of the race.

Loser: McLaren (8th & 14th)

A frustrating but solid race turned into a needlessly destructive one for McLaren thanks to Lando Norris’s over-ambitious final lap move.

Sending it down the inside of Turn 5 in the wet is borderline desperate at the best of times, let alone against your team-mate.

McLaren chiefs must have been holding their breath when it happened but ultimately, while gutted, surely not surprised that it caused a synchronised pirouette from the pair, ending Oscar Piastri’s race in the process.

It was always likely to end badly and it could yet get worse if Norris cops a penalty for it that loses him eighth place, and with it the measly point McLaren still got as a weak silver lining.

Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)

Would Verstappen have had anything to come back at Russell with? We'll never know - though you could infer that Verstappen might've found it difficult considering his assertion post-race that "I think we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass".

That's all academic. Verstappen never looked under threat from behind, and his drive to victory had an air of cruise control to it - at a track, too, where Verstappen can struggle to reach his peak level of performance.

Yet more evidence that the four-time champion is the form driver right now.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (DNF)

It's hard to judge Hadjar too harshly considering he managed only two laps before parking up with a power issue.

But he did lose two places at the start, if we're being ultra-critical.

And of course, there's no escaping the fact this was a DNF in a race won by the sister car.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (2nd)

Lewis Hamilton did the hard work for his sprint race in the opening few seconds, leaping forward past his team-mate and the two McLarens.

Considering he seemed to have the best pace of anyone besides Verstappen in this race, that was critical. Getting stuck on a track where it looked almost impossible to overtake in these conditions - barring bigger pace swings in the midfield - would have made Hamilton’s sprint look a lot more average.

He couldn't quite match Verstappen in the middle of the race but started to whittle away at the lead again late on and was much, much better managing his tyres than team-mate Leclerc seemed to be as the track dried.

Winner: Liam Lawson (5th)

If you can keep your head when all around you are losing theirs...

OK, the Singapore sprint wasn't the most difficult to navigate in reality, but there was still plenty of reward to be reaped from keeping it neat and tidy.

This was another exemplary drive from Lawson, who in repeating his best-of-the-rest trick from qualifying also stood to gain from any incidents up ahead. (Hello, McLaren.)

It's this sort of drive that means the direction of travel is only going one way in the fight for fifth in the constructors' championship between Racing Bulls and Alpine right now.

Loser: Arvid Lindblad (13th)

Compare Lawson's serene run to fifth with Racing Bulls team-mate Lindblad's travails.

Lindblad was perplexed after the race by his spin under the safety car - "it was a bit confusing at the time because it was pretty gentle on power, then just suddenly lost it" - but was a little loose in his description of events that "then I tried to just get it back round", as he in fact had spent multiple seconds driving the car backwards while trying to loop around at Turn 5.

No surprise then that that caught the attention of race control.

And even if he escapes penalty, this was a last-on-the-road finish in the same car that finished well up the road in fifth. There's no question, considering the attrition, that points were up for grabs.

Loser: Cadillac (DNF & DNF)

Two cars. Two collisions. One unproductive race.

The Sergio Perez-Lance Stroll clash looked like as clear a case of racing incident as you'll find, so there's little blame to be apportioned to the Cadillac driver there.

Valtteri Bottas doesn't get such an easy ride. What initially looked like a lazy slide from Alex Albon into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto was actually the result of Bottas getting into the back of the Williams. All this before the race had restarted, too.

The "rubber band" effect was partly to blame - Bottas said "the two cars ahead of me came to full stop and I just didn't have time to react" - but he did ultimately trigger contact.

So much for this being the sort of weekend, and track, that can play into Cadillac's hands...

Winner: Ollie Bearman (6th)

Ollie Bearman was absolutely thrilled with his work in the sprint, even though he acknowledged his seven-place rise was bolstered by others screwing up.

Irrespective of the Russell shunt and McLaren collision, though, Bearman was a man on the move here. He toughed it out nicely to get ahead of Pierre Gasly once the race resumed post-safety car, and that was critical for consolidating a points finish.

Bearman was on course to grab eighth irrespective of what happened on the final lap - so the bump up to sixth merely boosted the Haas driver rather than flattered his efforts completely.

items.title: ‘People Are Dying’: Riders Delay Il Lombardia in Rare Public Protest Over Safety
items.author: ahood
items.content: A frustrated peloton stages a five-minute protest and issues a joint statement demanding tighter course security and action from the UCI and race organizers.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel, shown here with world champion Brandon McNulty, spoke out on behalf of the peloton over rider safety. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

The riders have had enough, and the bunch delayed Il Lombardia for five minutes Saturday morning to demand safer roads after another ugly week of vehicles getting onto race courses .

World champion Brandon McNulty and European champion Remco Evenepoel stood at the front as the peloton held up the season’s final monument to demand rider safety .

Evenepoel grabbed the microphone and spoke for the riders in a rare public showing of solidarity.

“In the name of the whole bunch and not only for the guys that are here but for everybody pro cycling, we want to make this statement because there’s too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race,” Evenepoel said.

“Unfortunately, we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us,” he said. “We want to make this statement to just show to the whole world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured and are literally dying while doing what we like the most.”

The riders and the CPA also issued a joint statement asking the UCI and race organizers to take responsibility and tighten course security ( see statement below ).

Frustration has been bubbling behind the scenes ever since 19-year-old Finlay Tarling was killed following a collision with a vehicle that entered the Volta a Portugal course in August.

Michael Tarling, the father of Finlay, took to X to support the solidarity among the riders.

“We are so thankful, moved and proud of Fin’s fellow cyclists today for making a stand at the Tour of Lombardy,” he wrote. “Things need to change and no other family should ever receive the phone call we received on 14th Aug. We sincerely hope the UCI are listening and changes will be made.”

‼️ La protesta del pelotón, encabezada por Remco Evenepoel, antes del inicio de #IlLombardia ⚠️ El movimiento llega tras los últimos incidentes con vehículos de carrera estas semanas #LaCasadelCiclismo pic.twitter.com/OgEwYGlIwq

Saturday’s protest comes on the heels of high-profile vehicle incidents at both Coppa Bernocchi and Tre Valli Varesine this week in Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi, a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route from a side street and drove behind the breakaway before stopping.

A day later, a police motorbike traveling against the direction of racing collided with Tom Pidcock’s Pinarello-Q36.5 teammates Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubí at Tre Valli Varesine.

Gloag abandoned and required stitches to his knee , while Camprubí continued and later complained that “nothing changes.”

Heavy crashes have marked racing this week in Italy as well .

The latest incidents add to a grim toll the past few years. Gino Mäder died after crashing at the 2023 Tour de Suisse, André Drege died while descending at the Tour of Austria in 2024, and junior racer Muriel Furrer died following a crash at the 2024 UCI Road World Championships.

“This is why we want to stand for five minutes more, to make our statement towards organizations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling and accepting the fact that people are dying,” Evenepoel said.

The UCI has introduced new safety measures , including better barriers and signage, but riders want faster action and stronger protection on race roads.

“We want to pay our tribute and respect to everybody that was already involved in the incidents,” he said.

After the protest, the race started without further incident.

There was no immediate response from the UCI.

As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to.

This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer.

Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

We are calling for the help of the UCI for race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one.

We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones.

items.lbText:
How will Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options

The sense of desperation will be strong as Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur arrive at Old Trafford with both teams in bad need of a win to change the narrative around their disappointing seasons so far.

Anything less than three points would further increase the pressure on Michael Carrick and Roberto De Zerbi , both of whom are fighting to prove they are the right people for their respective jobs. Saturday’s match could be pivotal.

Spurs can take encouragement from the fact they have won four of their last six encounters with United in all competitions dating back to September 2024. Less positive is their run of four blanks in the five league matches they have played so far this season.

Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.

United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports Main Event

Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur have suffered many of the same problems to start the season. Both teams have conceded far too many goals and struggled for any sort of defensive foundation. The former have yet to keep a single clean sheet in five league games while the latter have kept just two.

In midfield, Carrick and De Zerbi struggling for the right balance. Manchester United and Spurs both bought expensive new midfielders in the summer transfer window who have yet to settle into their new surroundings.

Things haven’t been much better in the attacking third where Spurs have scored in just one of their five league games. For Manchester United, the likes of Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Bryan Mbeumo have yet to find top form. This match could be a catalyst, but it’s not clear for whom.

Player to watch: Kobbie Mainoo, Manchester United – The 21-year-old has been United’s best player in the early part of the campaign and will be central to the home team gaining traction through the middle of the pitch. Mainoo could control the game.

items.title: Three winners and three losers from Knicks’ first two preseason games
items.author: Kento Kato
items.content:
The Knicks are back to playing basketball and are less than two weeks away from opening night. They’ve started 0-2, which nobody really cares about, but we’ve also now seen enough minutes from the exhibition matches to get a glimpse of who the winners and losers have been in the early portion of the preseason.

Winner: Jalen Brunson and his wrist

Should anyone have really doubted or even been remotely worried about Brunson’s offseason wrist surgery? No, the captain has repeatedly been the definition of reliable. So it was ridiculous to ever think that Brunson wouldn’t be prepared or would look off coming off of his injury. But fans are unreasonable. And also, he is a 30 year-old who had an operation on his shooting hand.

Fortunately for Knicks fans, though, he’s looked as good as any other Knicks. His three-point shot was off against the Wizards as he went just 1-for-6. But Brunson looks like he’s in midseason form. He’s taking his usual shots, which include, but aren’t limited to, driving layups, floaters, mid-range fadeaways, and pull-up threes, and he’s looked comfortable and confident in doing so. Defensively, he’s started the preseason giving good effort, and he’s already drawn multiple charges as well. Brunson and his wrist seem to be doing just fine.

Loser: Pacome Dadiet and his trade value

Coming into training camp and preseason, there couldn’t have been many expectations for Dadiet. He’s now had two full seasons of pretty much being non-existent. His Summer League left a lot to be desired. And he played worse than most fans could’ve imagined during the World Cup qualifiers for the Ivory Coast team. Yet even after all that, he’s found a way to disappoint so far in preseason. In the preseason opener, the team was clearly trying to give him an opportunity to either increase his trade value or at least win some spot minutes, and he failed to do that. And he wasn’t much better in game two against the Wizards.

It’s only been two games, but they’ve both been a failure for Dadiet. He’s scored just nine total points in 30 minutes of play and is shooting just 28.6% from the field without standing out as a playmaker, rebounder, or defender. Dadiet’s path to being a rotation player in New York was pretty thin to begin with. But whatever opportunity he had to at least help the team out by increasing his trade value may be slipping away now too.

Shamet is coming off of two straight training camps where his job wasn’t even guaranteed. He’s battled back from injuries and has consistently displayed a perfect balance of selflessness and staying ready. That led to him becoming an integral part of the Knicks’ rotation last year. And he was rewarded with a very nice four-year, $24 million contract. Shamet rewarded the Knicks and their loyalty by reportedly turning down offers from other contenders.

Now back with the same team for the third straight year-something he’s never done before in his career-the journeyman looks comfortable and confident. He looks poised to not just continue what he’s done but build upon it and has gotten off to an extremely hot start in preseason. He’s averaging 11.5PPG in just 13.5MPG and is shooting an extremely hot 53.3% from the field and 50% from three.

The talk around McBride for much of the offseason has been about what the Knicks could get in a trade for him. And after the offensive struggles he went through in the Finals, there are some fans who may have forgotten just how good and valuable the reserve guard is. He’s still one of the best bench perimeter defenders in the league, and that, combined with his much improved three-point shooting, makes him so pivotal to what Mike Brown and the Knicks want to do. And nobody should be overly concerned about what he does or doesn’t do in the preseason.

That being said, he’s currently struggling mightily offensively. McBride has so far averaged just 3PPG on 18.2% shooting from the field and 11.1% shooting from three. There were some expectations that he’d showcase a little more after a full offseason to work on some of his weaknesses that got exposed against the Spurs. And fans were excited to see him fully healthy after he revealed that he was still hurt throughout the postseason run. He should be fine eventually, but it’s been a rough go for McBride so far.

Many fans had different reactions when Drummond signed with the Knicks this past summer. Some were excited, some were indifferent, and some were disappointed. New York still has a very long season ahead of them, and that should come with opportunities to upgrade at this position one way or another. And during said long season, Drummond will inevitably go through ups and downs. But so far, the veteran center has looked solid.

His pick-and-roll defense, something many were concerned about, has actually looked good. He’s been very active with his hands, and his defense there, especially when paired up with the also active Jose Alvarado, could be a fun tandem. Drummond’s finishing ability is concerning due to his lack of explosiveness. But his surprisingly solid defense, along with his elite-as-advertised rebounding, has been fun to watch.

Losers: Drew Eubanks, Ochai Agbaji, and Tony Bradley

Bruce Brown Jr. was looked at as one of the favorites to win the Knicks’ last roster spot given the team’s previous interest in him. Other than that, there really wasn’t a consensus. Some wanted James Wiseman for his potential. Others wanted Eubanks for his defense, passing, and experience. Others wanted Agbaji for… not really sure why.

Two games into preseason, it looks clear who Brown and the Knicks have the most interest in. Brown, Wiseman, and Jaden Akins are the only three of the training camp invitees to play in both games. On Thursday night against the Wizards, Eubanks, Agbaji, and Bradley were DNPs. Now, this may just be the way they are splitting up the minutes, and maybe those guys see minutes over Brown and Wiseman when they play the Timberwolves on Monday. Brown, although not overly impressive, has looked solid. And Wiseman, especially against the 76ers, looked good. Neither is locked in to make the roster just yet. But it seems like they are a head above Eubanks, Agbaji, and Bradley.

items.title: Bauke Mollema, Pello Bilbao and other retiring riders receive guard of honour send-off at Il Lombardia
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
The retiring riders for whom Il Lombardia will be their final race received a warm send-off and a guard of honour from the peloton at the start of the Italian Monument in Bergamo on Saturday morning.

Multiple riders are closing the curtain on their careers in Italy this Saturday, including former winner Bauke Mollema (Lidl-Trek), plus Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious), Rudy Molard (Groupama-FDJ United), Odd Christian Eiking (Unibet Rose Rockets) and Ion Izagirre (Cofidis).

At the start, the retirees were presented with a guard of honour from their peloton colleagues, who lined the road with their bikes in the air to wave off the departing riders.

Mollema, who won this race in 2019 and has the most starts in the current peloton with a whopping 17, was also presented with a medal and framed plaque on stage during the team sign-on to commemorate the last race of his career.

This comes alongside a special Netherlands-themed paint job on his Trek bike for his final race.

"There's quite a lot going through my mind today, it's a special day, ending my career here in Lombardia, in a race that I won and that has given me a lot," the Dutchman told at the start.

"It's been a long journey, almost 20 years in professional cycling, and today is the last day, in a race I love. I've always loved to race in Italy, so I hope to enjoy it a bit, but it will also be a lot of suffering."

items.title: Verstappen wins delayed Singapore sprint, Russell crashes from lead
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Max Verstappen won an attritional Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix sprint race bookended by initial race leader George Russell crashing out and the two McLarens colliding.

After a delayed start due to heavy rain in the build-up to the sprint, Russell jumped Verstappen into the first corner - but his lead barely lasted a full lap.

The Mercedes driver, for whom a win might have barely kept alive his faint title hopes, spun exiting the final corner and crashed into the pitwall just beyond the timing line.

That freed up Verstappen to take a controlled victory (after a safety car period) in which he steadily built his lead over Lewis Hamilton and managed it easily until the end.

Hamilton’s second place was earned from a lightning start that vaulted him ahead of both McLarens and his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

And he was clearly the faster Ferrari in these conditions as Leclerc faded extremely badly late on, putting him under pressure from Oscar Piastri, Lando Norris and a muted championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Leclerc looked to have done enough to stave off the McLaren threat even before they collided calamitously on the final lap.

Norris launched a silly move on his team-mate into the Turn 5 right-hander. Piastri left some room on the inside but Norris, who went over the kerb, hit his team-mate's car and spun both of them round.

Though Norris rejoined after a short delay and claimed a point in eighth - a point he may lose given the incident is under investigation - Piastri retired in the wall.

This gifted Antonelli fourth and elevated several midfield cars into healthy points positions.

Liam Lawson spearheaded this group with a very accomplished drive to fifth while Ollie Bearman was sixth for Haas - keeping Nico Hulkenberg from his team’s championship rival Audi at bay in the process.

Hulkenberg had robustly passed Pierre Gasly earlier in the race to run behind Bearman but looked set to end the sprint empty-handed before McLaren imploded.

Among the nine retirees were also Isack Hadjar and Franco Colapinto, who suffered stoppages during the early safety car period, first-lap colliders Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez, and Alex Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas.

Albon and Bortoleto collided ahead of the safety car period ending in an incident that will be investigated after the race.

items.title: 'I just had nothing to lose' – Tiffany Cromwell delivers feisty farewell in Nannup at home UCI Gravel World Championships
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
The Australian rider has won at the SEVEN Gravel World Series race held in the same location three times, and she was going to make the most of that home advantage to time her moves.

"When you know it's your last one, the head space was good. I knew I just had nothing to lose," Cromwell told after crossing her final finish line.

The outcome was eighth as she took on her fifth and final Gravel Worlds, but she carved out a spectacular path along the way. The first key selection, as expected, was made on Brockman and Cromwell became part of the chase group, which through the next section just kept chipping away at the gap. Cromwell finally closed the last bit and rather than sitting in, decided she may as well just keep on going.

"In gravel, I've always been good at just getting in my rhythm, and I think just the dynamic at the front – nobody really wants to show their cards too quickly – it seemed to play into my favour."

Initially it looked like Cromwell's move would be short-lived, with Marianne Vos (Netherlands) among those to go out in pursuit, but then her rivals started looking at each other and the gap stretched, sitting at over a minute at 70km to go in the 125.6km race with 3,179m of elevation gain.

"It was obviously early on but It was like 'OK, you know, why not try something, get a head start," she said, who knew that she "always suffered" on the Ellis climb ahead.

"Getting that far and having the head start was perfect because then it put me really back in the game.

"I knew I couldn't match the girls on the climb, so I just had to take a chance, and I think it was just one of those days, you're just not thinking, you're not doubting yourself."

So even though she was caught, dropped and then clawed her way back again once more it was Cromwell who was charging into the brutal climb of Folly with just under 30km to go, delivering an excited roar and chatter from among the waiting crowd who hadn't been expecting her to be on the charge, or perhaps even in the lead group, once again.

"I was like, 'I'm cooked, I could sit here, get dropped in a few k or attack," she said. "And the way gravel works, a lot of individual riders against each other, nobody wants to necessarily chase straight away, so again, it just gave me another head start for Folly. But then I was like, done, done."

Though she still held on for a finish within the top ten, even sprinting to the line against Elisa Serné (Netherlands) to make sure she got eight and not ninth.

"I wanted to come here, race my bike, give everything I had, and just be at the finish having no regrets," concluded Cromwell as she did her final round of post-race media interviews to conclude a career spanning 17 seasons, and with a bank of many successes – which now includes her second UCI Gravel World Championships top 10.

items.title: Marianne Vos Wins UCI Gravel Worlds, Gomez Villafañe Sixth, Heavy Crash Mars Race
items.author: ahood
items.content: Results: Vos claims her second gravel world title at thrilling first edition outside Europe, Geerike Schreurs involved in a heavy crash.
items.lbText:
Vos, pictured here in the 2024 edition, won her second UCI gravel worlds title in a wild race Saturday. (Photo: JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga via AFP)

Marianne Vos claimed a second UCI Gravel World Championship title Saturday in Nannup, Australia, winning solo after a showdown with Rosa Klöser as U.S.-based gravel star Sofia Gomez Villafañe finished sixth.

A heavy crash involving Geerike Schreurs and Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio overshadowed the race.

“This victory really means a lot to me,” Vos said.

Germany’s Klöser finished 27 seconds behind Vos after slipping out in the closing kilometers. Larissa Hartog took bronze for the Netherlands.

Gomez Villafañe, representing Argentina, crossed the line sixth at 5:15 back. Tiffany Cromwell, racing in her final pro race , attacked early before finishing eighth.

Vos and Klöser pulled clear late in the race to chase the rainbow jersey.

Vos, 39, accelerated inside the final four kilometers, and Klöser fought back onto her wheel before sliding out. The Dutchwoman soloed to the line to win her career 15th world title across different disciplines.

“There was more mud than I expected. As a result, there were also some slippery sections on the course, so we had to be careful at times. Rosa was incredibly strong, especially on the climbs, where I really had to dig deep to stay with her,” Vos said.

Nannup’s punishing 125.6km course with about 3,180m of climbing is the first gravel worlds held outside Europe .

The race started after a controversial late-hour UCI decision over points that impacted dozens of riders .

Cromwell gave the locals something to cheer about when she attacked early. The favorites organized a chase behind as Cromwell opened up a gap of 1:30.

Schreurs was involved in a heavy crash with about 70km to go.

The Dutch woman lost control while riding near the front of the chasing group, went off the gravel road, and hit the ground hard.

"She has not moved." "She’s badly hit her head." 🇿🇦 Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio and 🇳🇱 Geerike Schreurs suffered heavy falls in the elite women’s race, with red flags raised following the incidents. #NannupGravel2026 | October 10-11 | SBS & SBS On Demand 📺 pic.twitter.com/mXPa1JhJBT

Moolman-Pasio, also racing her final pro race , also crashed and remained nearby as medical staff attended to the Dutch rider. There was no immediate update on possible injuries.

Vos and Klöser caught Cromwell with about 24km to go and opened up a winning gap coming into the final 10km. Klöser slipped out on a corner, and Vos drove home the victory in a wild finale.

“It was a fantastic course here in Australia. I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here,” she said.

Vos now owns 15 elite world titles across four disciplines: eight in cyclocross, three on the road, two on the track and, with her win in Australia, two in gravel.

items.title: Sprint start crash causes huge tension within Aprilia
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Raul Fernandez has repeatedly excoriated Aprilia stablemate Marco Bezzecchi for his role in setting up their crash at the start of the Mandalika sprint, describing Bezzecchi's tactics as "not nice", "ungentlemanly" and "not clever".

Fernandez fractured his left index finger in the crash at the start of the sprint, which was triggered as four riders - Fernandez, Bezzecchi, Marc Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio - went into Turn 1 almost side-by-side and their lines converged deep into the corner.

As Di Giannantonio ran Marquez out wide, Bezzecchi checked up and had contact with Fernandez that took both out of the race and injured the latter. Fernandez is now in doubt for the grand prix, but will try to contest the warm-up.

Fernandez was seething after the sprint, giving explosive interviews to both Spanish broadcaster DAZN and Italian broadcaster Sky Sport, in which he effectively accused Bezzecchi of deliberately compromising his race at the cost of letting two Ducatis through.

His tone softened between the TV interviews and the written media, but his argument remained the same. Bezzecchi, he felt, approached Turn 1 with the focus only on beating Fernandez, squeezed him out and left the door open for the two Ducatis, which created the conditions for the crash.

"For me, the crash is a consequence of the start," Fernandez said. "On the start, for me I tried to keep my bike in the middle of the track, to try to not open the door for other riders to overtake. Marco had made a really good start and he overtook me - he didn't really overtake 100 percent, but he put the bike close to me and started to take me out the track.

"And this is for me the more frustrating thing about today. When you want to do something that is not clean in this sport. We are riders, we put our body [on the line] at more than 300km/h and when you are doing something that you know that is not really nice, I am not happy with that.

"And for me the version is, OK, we crash, it doesn't matter, it can happen, one day it will be me that I will make a mistake, another day will be another rider. The problem is when you are making something that you know is not nice. And for me this is the big problem that we saw today.

"We go out [wide] he doesn't give me space, two Ducatis overtook us, we crash, that's it."

Fernandez chuckled that it was "for sure not good" as a strategy by Bezzecchi. He said the Aprilia riders knew the battle for victory would play out between them, and accused Bezzecchi of "thinking just of me".

"I am not playing for the championship. He was playing for the championship. For me he was not very smart."

He also indicated he was more upset with Bezzecchi over this than with Jorge Martin over the Balaton Park pile-up at Turn 1, as that had been a mere mistake and this was a premeditated "bad action to another rider".

He said it was nothing that could or should be penalised but that Bezzecchi "didn't have the respect" and that, while Aprilia riders are told to be "gentlemen" with one another in terms of wheel-to-wheel racing, it "looks like he [Bezzecchi] was not a gentleman with us".

Bezzecchi defends himself

Bezzecchi was told of Fernandez's incandescence but chalked it up to heat-of-the-moment emotions clouding Fernandez's judgment. "I am maybe the one who can confirm this more than anyone," he joked, in seeming reference to his ban at Assen for striking a marshal.

It was a "racing incident", Bezzecchi insisted. "I was just looking to put myself in the best place possible for the braking. I knew Marc could try to overtake but was for me useless to try to force too much and maybe throw away the race in the first corner.

"It's what I did. If Raul is angry, I'm sorry, but honestly, he touched me! So at the end there's nothing to be angry for. Me versus him or him versus me, at the end it was a racing incident. I couldn't disappear and he also couldn't disappear. I don't want to waste energy with this, I want to focus for tomorrow."

How the Ducati pair saw it

Marquez, who went on to win the sprint, said the incident was "easy to explain".

"Four bikes in parallel, and I believe that Bezzecchi was looking at Raul, to brake a bit later, I was looking at Bezzecchi to brake a bit later, and Diggia was looking at me to brake a bit later. The consequence - four riders out of the line and [Jorge] Martin from fifth to first," he recounted.

Di Giannantonio had been completely unaware that anyone had crashed - but did say that contact with Marquez coming through the corner caused a downshift on his end that then compromised his exit from Turn 1.

"Honestly, you have to ask the others [about the incident] - me, I just got hit again."

items.title: 'At the end of the day, you can only try' – Despite puncture and a late crash, Rosa Klöser claws back silver at UCI Gravel World Championships
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
It was just 20km into the UCI Gravel World Championships elite women's race on Saturday and Rosa Klöser (Germany) thought it may have already been over, when a tricky flat dropped her out of the lead group not long before the first crucial climb of the day.

But somehow, some 100km later, she was out front with Marianne Vos (Netherlands) and contending for the win.

"It was definitely a tough race. I mean, the course is really relentless," Klöser told after going to the podium to claim her silver medal.

The bad luck also seemed to be just as relentless for the rider wearing the number 13 on her back, as it turned out her flat tyre wouldn't be the only misfortune of her day.

"It was a really big job for me to come back because it was also not easy to find the hole in my tyre, so it took me really quite a while until I got going again," said Klöser. "And if I'm honest, I saw the race move away from me there, but I was like, 'OK, you know what, you can only try'. So I kept pushing, and when I could see them I got an extra gear and I managed to come back to the front group,"

The front group ebbed and flowed as groups rejoined and then were again shed on the unrelenting course and a caught stick caused another quick stop for Klöser , that, however was quickly dealt with and the Canyon-SRAM-MAAP rider went with Vos at around 20km to go

Once she made it, however, her travails weren't over, with a stick caught in her rear mech, but that barely made a dent compared to the other chase back which could well have weakened her sprint.

Klöser, who has also spent a considerable amount of time on the road this year, jumped back into gravel with a couple of UCI Gravel World Series races in September, winning both and in one of them, Sea Otter Europe, shaking off Vos. It's clear that Klöser was coming into the race with a course that seemed to suit her and some powerful form.

"I won't lie, it was a really big goal," said Kloser, who did have her season interrupted by a parasitic infection that she was unaware of, but worked it out in time to prepare for the rainbow jersey race.

As the final 10km approached, it looked set to come down to a sprint battle between Vos, who is renowned for her prowess in delivering a sprint finish at the end of a tough race, and Klöser, who managed to pull off a huge gravel win when she clinched Unbound in a sprint of nine. But more bad luck struck before Klöser could even think about the sprint.

"Unfortunately, I think with 4km to go, I wiped out in like the last technical corner," said the rider who fronted up for the podium ceremonies and post-race interviews with a ripped shorts, a wound on one leg and a banged-up arm.

"I probably overinflated my tyre also a bit when when it got flat. But I mean that's racing, that's gravel. At the end of the day, you can only try."
